metadata.title: Relationships Between Response Styles and the Hofstede and GLOBE Dimensions of Culture in a Sample of Adolescents From 33 Countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study is a secondary, country-level analysis using Buckley (2009) mean response-style estimates derived from PISA 2006 student questionnaire data. The paper does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures in its own correlation/partial-correlation analyses, and it instead uses already-aggregated country means for response styles and externally sourced country indices (Hofstede and GLOBE) plus GDP per capita. Because the dependent variables are country-level averages rather than individual student PV-based achievement scores, the paper does not describe any PV estimation or complex-survey variance estimation steps. Consequently, weighting is not documented as part of the authors’ analytic workflow, and any representativeness adjustments are implicitly embedded in the earlier response-style estimation work rather than re-applied here.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are country-level mean response-style indices (ERS, ARS, DARS, NONC) adopted from Buckley (2009), not cognitive achievement scores with PISA plausible values. As a result, plausible-value generation/combining is not applicable to the analyses reported here. The paper also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure for the country-level indices (e.g., how missing country scores would be treated), which is a reporting gap given that the analysis is restricted to 33 countries with available Hofstede and GLOBE scores.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses secondary, country-level data: mean response-style estimates (ERS, ARS, DARS, NONC) for 15-year-olds from PISA 2006, as computed by Buckley (2009). The authors restrict the country set to 33 PISA 2006 countries that have validated Hofstede scores and available GLOBE practice-dimension scores, explicitly excluding Japan due to response-style outlier status. The paper does not report additional student-level inclusion/exclusion beyond the fact that response styles were derived from PISA 2006 science-attitude questionnaire items and then aggregated to country means.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2006 (15-year-olds) country-level response-style data across 33 countries, the study leveraged Hofstede uncertainty avoidance, GLOBE humane orientation, GLOBE assertiveness, and country GDP per capita to analyze non-contingent response style (NONC), finding that NONC shows no significant simple association with GDP per capita but is strongly related to cultural dimensions—especially higher Hofstede uncertainty avoidance and higher GLOBE assertiveness, alongside lower GLOBE humane orientation and lower GLOBE institutional collectivism. This indicates that careless or unintentional responding patterns in adolescent surveys may be culturally patterned in ways that are not reducible to national wealth alone, supporting the need to incorporate cultural context when comparing questionnaire response quality across countries.

data.outcome_summary: The study conducts secondary, country-level analyses using PISA 2006 (15-year-olds) response-style estimates (ERS, ARS, DARS, NONC) from Buckley (2009) for 33 countries. It reports Pearson correlations between response styles and country GDP per capita, and correlations between response styles and Hofstede (6) and GLOBE (9) cultural indices, then repeats these relationships as partial correlations holding GDP per capita constant. Across Table 1 and Table 2, GDP per capita is negatively associated with ARS (r = −.377, p<.05) and positively associated with DARS (r = .430, p<.05), while it is not significantly related to ERS or NONC. Several cultural associations weaken or change sign after GDP adjustment (notably Hofstede individualism with DARS and some GLOBE uncertainty/future orientation links), while others remain robust (e.g., Hofstede uncertainty avoidance with NONC; GLOBE power distance with ERS/ARS). The paper uses correlation/partial-correlation rather than ML, so no predictive performance metrics or survey-weighted estimation are reported, and the findings are associational and country-aggregated.
